summary: The note traces the origins of wedding rings to Ancient Egypt, where braided rings of hemp or reeds were exchanged between spouses as a symbol of perpetual love. It notes that Western customs descend from ancient Rome and Greece and were carried forward through Christendom in Europe. It also explains the belief behind wearing the ring on the left ring finger, linked to a vein thought to run directly to the heart.
one_line: Overview of the history of wedding rings, from braided Egyptian rings through Roman, Greek and European customs.
key_facts: The earliest examples of wedding rings are from Ancient Egypt.
Western wedding ring customs can be traced to ancient Rome and Greece.
Western customs were transmitted to the present through Christendom in Europe, which adapted the ancient customs.
It is commonly believed that the first examples of wedding rings were found in ancient Egypt.
Relics dating to 6,000 years ago, including papyrus scrolls, are evidence of the exchange of braided rings of hemp or reeds between spouses.
Ancient Egypt considered the circle to be a symbol of eternity.
In ancient Egypt, the ring served to signify the perpetual love of the spouses.
The custom of wearing the wedding ring on the ring finger of the left hand originated in ancient Egypt.
Ancient Egyptians believed the left ring finger enclosed a special vein connected directly to the heart.
The vein was denominated in Latin the "Vena amoris".
